title: Paul taught that Antichrist comes before the Lord — not the date; the restrainer is in the letter
source_text: XX. Sed quod ad rem ipsam attinet, Apostolus non innuit se docuisse Thessalonicenses quando venturus esset Antichristus, sed simpliciter illum venturum esse ante secundum Domini adventum, ac praeterea quid tardaret Antichristi adventum. Et enim non dicit, scitis quo tempore venturus est homo peccati, sed simpliciter, nunc quid detineat scitis. Quid autem esset illud, non tantum viva voce docuerat ante Apostolus, sed postea repetit & confirmat in hac ipsa epistola, Tantum enim, inquit, qui nunc retinet, retinebit, usque dum e medio tollatur: Et tunc revelabitur iniquus ille. Obscure ista quidem, quae forsan clarius & uberius viva voce explicuerat Paulus, sed quicquid sit traditio nihil hic ad Scripturam adjicit, neque ex ea habemus quicquam amplius de iis quae paullo innuit Apostolus.
pass_a_gloss: But as for the matter itself, the Apostle does not hint that he taught the Thessalonians when the Antichrist would come, but simply that he would come before the second advent of the Lord, and besides what would delay the coming of the Antichrist. For he does not say, you know at what time the man of sin is to come, but simply, now you know what restrains. But what that was, the Apostle had not only taught before by living voice, but afterward repeats and confirms in this very epistle, For only, he says, he who now restrains will restrain, until he is taken out of the way: And then that wicked one will be revealed. These things are indeed obscure, which perhaps Paul had explained more clearly and fully by living voice, but whatever the case tradition adds nothing here to Scripture, nor do we have from it anything further concerning those things which the Apostle faintly hints.
pass_b_english: Paul did not teach a date — only that Antichrist comes before the Lord's return, and what delays him.
He says you know what restrains — not you know the hour of the man of sin.
The same restrainer is repeated in the letter itself until he is taken out of the way.
Oral clarity may have helped hearers; tradition still adds nothing beyond the written hint.
